To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of preliminary class membership are not limited to the stimuli that comprise the class, but also include the stimuli that were not trained as class members.

the effects of preliminary class formation on subsequent stimulus equivalence formation were minimal and that procedural variables in the preliminary phase accounted for more of the effects than the stimulus control functions of the preliminary class stimuli.

the effects of preliminary functional class training on subsequent class formation are more pronounced than the effects of preliminary equivalence class training and that preliminary training procedures, rather than stimulus control properties of acquired function stimuli, account for most of these effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of stimulus equivalence classes, and the effects of preliminary class membership in the formation of subsequent stimulus equivalence classes.
the role of preliminary training on subsequent class formation.
the development of equivalence class membership, and how the formation of such classes is affected by prior training.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, preliminary class membership does not facilitate subsequent class formation, but procedural aspects of preliminary training do.
the preliminary phase training of functional relations does not facilitate subsequent stimulus equivalence class acquisition.

the effects of preliminary class training on subsequent equivalence class acquisition are not as straightforward as previously thought, and that the stimulus control properties acquired during the preliminary training phase are not the only factor responsible for the effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of preliminary class membership are complex, but that the effects of the stimuli themselves are minimal.
the effects of preliminary functional and equivalence class training on subsequent equivalence class learning depend on procedural variables in preliminary class training.

preliminary training can be detrimental to class formation if it is too complex, but it is also possible to design preliminary training that is conducive to class formation, as demonstrated by the PIC results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the preliminary training procedures that we employed did not facilitate subsequent class formation.
the effects of preliminary class membership are not straightforward and depend on the type of training that precedes the terminal class formation task.

the effects of preliminary class membership may not be due to the stimulus control properties acquired in the preliminary training phase, but instead may be due to the procedural aspects of the preliminary training.
